advice: Bloat is a buildup of gas in the stomach, often from eating too much fresh legume feed. Keep the animal standing and walking if possible. This can become an emergency quickly.
Mastitis is an udder infection. Gently milk out the affected quarter and keep the area clean. Recovery is much better with early treatment.
Foot rot is a bacterial infection between the toes, common in wet or muddy conditions. Move the animal to a dry area and clean the foot if possible.
This is a highly contagious viral disease with no treatment. Isolate sick birds immediately from the rest of the flock to limit spread.
Similar to cattle bloat — gas buildup from feed changes. Encourage movement and monitor closely; this can escalate fast.
Ensure the animal has access to clean water to prevent dehydration. Persistent diarrhea over 2 days needs a vet check for parasites or infection.
These are classic signs of worm burden. Pale gums especially need attention soon, as heavy worm loads can be dangerous. A dewormer and vet check are recommended.
Fast or labored breathing combined with discharge and lethargy needs prompt attention — respiratory infections can worsen quickly, especially in young animals.
Keep the animal away from dust and flies, which worsen eye infections. Gently clean discharge with clean water. If cloudiness affects vision, see a vet soon.
A prolonged or stuck birth is dangerous for both mother and offspring and needs immediate hands-on help — this is not something to wait out.

condition: Egg production drop (nutrition or stress related)
advice: Sudden drops in egg laying are often linked to diet, heat stress, or lighting changes. Check feed quality and water access first.
Visible ticks or mite-related skin irritation should be treated promptly, as they can spread disease and cause anemia in heavy infestations.
